Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench:
From Direct Control to Harness with Policy

Yifei Yao  Yude Zou11footnotemark: 1  Guanbo Jiao11footnotemark: 1  Xing Gao  Ning Gao Yukai Wang  Jiantong Chen  Zihou Zhu  Xinyu Li  Ningyu Yan  Shuai Wang Jianming Ma  Haoyu Guo  Weinan Zhang  Chunhua Shen Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory  Shanghai Jiao Tong University Fudan University  Zhejiang University ††thanks: Equal contribution.  †Corresponding author: Xing Gao (gaoxing@pjlab.org.cn).
Abstract

Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/.

1 Introduction

Transferring knowledge from large pretrained models to robotics has become a primary approach to general-purpose robot control (Firoozi et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026b; Shen et al., 2026). Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt vision-language backbones for end-to-end visuomotor control (Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2026a; GigaBrain Team et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026a), whereas world action models (WAMs) jointly model future visual dynamics and actions to utilize the physical and temporal priors of video generative models (Ye et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b; Cai et al., 2026a). Both approaches rely on post-training with robot manipulation trajectories: although effective within their training distributions, their generalization is bounded by the scale and diversity of collected robot data. By contrast, frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) acquire stronger emergent capabilities from massive-scale pretraining data, and this training scale remains costly to replicate with embodied data alone.

Without robot-specific post-training, frontier MLLMs provide an alternative approach through their spatial understanding and embodied reasoning capabilities (Zhang et al., 2026a; Rao, 2026). GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026), for example, can generate end-effector (EEF) commands directly from camera observations and language instructions (Zhang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026; Jia et al., 2026; Lou et al., 2026). Combined with an agent harness that supplies its prompt, observation interface, and tools, the model serves as the core of an agent that controls the robot in closed loop, as formalized in Section 3. Beyond direct control, recent studies explore a harness with policy in which the agent invokes a post-trained policy for action execution (Zhang et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). Such a harness combines the agent’s task planning, progress monitoring, and error recovery with the closed-loop visuomotor control that the policy learns from robot demonstrations.

Although prior studies have evaluated both direct control and a harness with policy, they have not comprehensively profiled these agent configurations against post-trained VLA and WAM policies across diverse manipulation demands. Specifically, two central questions remain to be addressed. First, under direct control, on which tasks does the agent outperform post-trained VLAs and WAMs, where does it fall short, and what limits its performance? Second, in a harness-with-policy setting, how does invoking a post-trained policy complement the agent’s direct control, which limitations of direct control can it alleviate, and what new failure modes arise when the agent invokes a policy for execution and subsequently resumes decision-making?

To further explore these questions, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra as the core of an agent on EBench (Gao et al., 2026). This diagnostic manipulation benchmark categorizes tasks by mobility, manipulation precision, and task horizon and evaluates robustness along the generalization dimensions of unseen objects, unseen backgrounds, paraphrased instructions, and their mixture. For a fair comparison, the agent operates under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, receiving only RGB camera images and proprioceptive robot states without depth, camera calibration, or simulator ground truth. For each task, the agent receives a task description annotated by GPT-6-Astra from a single training episode as single-shot in-context learning (ICL). Across all 510 test episodes, we evaluate both direct control and a harness with policy invoking either the VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} or the WAM InternW0-Δ\Delta, compare each configuration against the post-trained policies on the EBench leaderboard, and analyze execution trajectories across paired episodes.

Under direct control, the GPT-6-Astra-based agent achieves a 46.7% overall success rate and a 0.654 stage-completion score, outperforming post-trained policies such as Qwen-RobotManip and π0.5\pi_{0.5} trained on 6,600 in-domain demonstrations. Among the compared post-trained policies, the agent ranks first on short-horizon tasks with a 73.2% success rate, shows the smallest success-rate variation across the four generalization dimensions, and completes a novel composite instruction zero-shot on which both compared post-trained policies fail. Conversely, its success rate drops to 27.3% on long-horizon tasks, 20.0% on tabletop manipulation, and 11.3% on high-precision contact-rich tasks. Trajectory analysis shows that while the agent performs well at visual grounding and in-episode error recovery, its physical execution is limited by long action chunks between observations and by contact geometry that it must infer explicitly from RGB views.

Invoking a post-trained policy through the agent harness increases the overall success rate to 53.0% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 56.0% with InternW0-Δ\Delta and reduces the agent’s token cost per success by more than half. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, the harness surpasses all post-trained policies compared in Table 1. The harness with policy retains the agent’s high success rate on short-horizon tasks and improves performance on long-horizon and bimanual tasks where the post-trained policy is competent. At the same time, case analysis identifies two limitations of the current harness with policy. First, neither component resolves high-precision contact-rich manipulation. Second, agent and policy coordinate loosely in three respects: the agent invokes the policy for most execution steps even on tasks where that policy alone rarely succeeds, the policy follows the fixed task instruction instead of the agent’s subgoal, and the agent often leaves a held grasp unmaintained when it resumes control after a policy invocation, which makes object drops more frequent.

The main contributions of this report are as follows:

  • •

    Paired evaluation across agent configurations and post-trained policies. Under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, we evaluate an GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control and in a harness with policy across all 510 EBench test episodes. We compare both agent configurations against standalone post-trained VLA and WAM policies across all task groups and generalization dimensions.

  • •

    Characterization of agent capabilities under direct control. We locate where the GPT-6-Astra-based agent leads or trails eight post-trained policies while using only a single annotated task demonstration and no parameter updates, trace its unsuccessful episodes to their failure mechanisms, and examine its in-episode adaptation, the safety of its execution, and its zero-shot composition of skills on a novel instruction. Together, these analyses show where the agent and the policies complement each other.

  • •

    Analysis of harness with policy and implications for agent harness design. We evaluate the harness with either policy against each of its components on every task, trace the episodes that newly fail under the harness and those that fail with both policies to their decisive incidents, and analyze the agent’s policy invocation and the resulting token cost. These analyses locate the remaining gap to the better component in policy invocation, subgoal passing, and grasp maintenance when the agent resumes control, which informs the design of future agent harnesses.

2 Related Work

Robot manipulation with foundation models.

Two lines of work apply foundation models to robot manipulation. Post-trained policies typically adapt foundation models on robot manipulation trajectories, including VLA models that fine-tune vision-language backbones for action prediction (Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a) and WAMs that jointly model future visual dynamics and actions (Ye et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026b; Miao et al., 2026). Direct control with frontier MLLMs, in contrast, uses frontier MLLMs as the cores of agents that control robots without parameter updates. Early approaches translate model predictions into robot motion through generated programs that call perception and control APIs (Liang et al., 2023) or through embodiment-specific semantic primitives (Chen et al., 2026), whereas more recent studies prompt MLLMs to output EEF or joint commands directly (Jia et al., 2026; Lou et al., 2026). On the RoboDojo benchmark, for example, GPT-6-Astra generates robot actions directly from observations (Zhang et al., 2026a), and providing in-context demonstration segments together with in-episode interaction history further improves task success (Liu et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026b). Rather than evaluating direct control in isolation, our work systematically compares GPT-6-Astra under direct control against post-trained VLA and WAM policies on EBench (Gao et al., 2026) by task group and generalization dimension, linking dimension-level performance to step-by-step execution trajectories.

Harness with policy.

Combining both lines, recent frameworks build hierarchical harnesses in which an agent with an MLLM core invokes post-trained policies for action execution (Qin et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026b). For instance, Harness VLA invokes a frozen VLA alongside scripted or analytical primitives (Zhang et al., 2026b), BATON coordinates long-horizon VLA execution through a transition-aware memory that verifies subtask entry and exit conditions (Xu et al., 2026), and HarnessPAI synthesizes task-specific control programs that invoke post-trained policies without online deliberation (Wang et al., 2026a). Related frameworks also adapt harness coordination logic, policy interfaces, or recovery tools during deployment (Tang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c; Ding et al., 2026). However, existing studies primarily evaluate each proposed harness as a single integrated system. In contrast, we evaluate the agent both under direct control and in a harness with policy, and compare both agent configurations against standalone VLA and WAM policies across the same test scenes under a fixed in-context protocol. This paired evaluation quantifies how the agent’s policy invocation decisions align with the standalone competence of the post-trained policy, and traces episode-level gains and losses to the agent’s direct control, policy execution, or the transitions between them.

3 Problem Formulation

To compare a frontier MLLM with post-trained policies on a common benchmark, we first define the agent and its harness, and then specify the two agent configurations evaluated in this study: direct control and harness with policy.

3.1 Agent and Agent Harness

An agent (F,H)(F,H) consists of an MLLM core FF and an agent harness H=(pH,𝒪H,𝒯H)H=(p_{H},\mathcal{O}_{H},\mathcal{T}_{H}) through which it controls a robot. In this formulation, the prompt pHp_{H} specifies the robot, the rules of interaction, and the use of each tool. The observation interface 𝒪H\mathcal{O}_{H} determines which sensor readings and robot states reach the core, and the tool set 𝒯H\mathcal{T}_{H} lists the calls available to the core together with how each is executed. Because the harness runs the decision loop, executing each call and returning its result to the core, the agent defines a closed-loop policy πA\pi_{A} without robot-specific post-training of its core. For a task τ\tau on an episode scene ss with language instruction ℓs\ell_{s} and task context cτc_{\tau}, at each decision step tt the agent issues a tool call ata_{t} conditioned on the episode interaction history ht=(o1,a1,…,ot)h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,o_{t}), where o1o_{1} is the initial observation and each later oto_{t} is the result returned for at−1a_{t-1}:

at∼πA(⋅∣ht,ℓs,cτ),at∈𝒜H∪{stop},𝒜H=𝒜Hact∪𝒜Hinfo,a_{t}\sim\pi_{A}\big(\cdot\mid h_{t},\,\ell_{s},\,c_{\tau}\big),\qquad a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{H}\cup\{\texttt{stop}\},\qquad\mathcal{A}_{H}=\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{act}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{info}}, (1)

where 𝒜H\mathcal{A}_{H} contains the calls of the tools in 𝒯H\mathcal{T}_{H} with their admissible arguments. A call in 𝒜Hact\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{act}} advances the physics, either by commanding the robot through joint or EEF targets, gripper commands, motion primitives, or programs that compose them, or by invoking a controller such as a post-trained policy for a requested number of physics steps, and returns an updated observation through 𝒪H\mathcal{O}_{H}. A call in 𝒜Hinfo\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{info}} returns information without advancing the physics, such as the current camera views and robot state or a stored demonstration. Agent control ends when the agent issues stop or reaches the physics-step limit. Unlike post-trained VLA and WAM policies that learn visuomotor control through parameter updates on robot trajectories, the agent adapts online solely through in-context conditioning, visual and proprioceptive observations, and tool calls.

3.2 Direct Control and Harness with Policy

The two agent configurations evaluated in this study share the observation interface 𝒪H\mathcal{O}_{H} and differ in the tool calls 𝒜H\mathcal{A}_{H} exposed by the agent harness. Under direct control, 𝒜Hact=𝒜EEF\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{act}}=\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EEF}}, which consists of EEF, base, and gripper commands, and 𝒜Hinfo\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{info}} contains only a call that returns the current views and robot state, so the agent generates all motion commands itself. Under harness with policy, following Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b), the harness expands the action set to 𝒜Hact=𝒜EEF∪𝒜pol\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{act}}=\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{EEF}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{pol}}, where 𝒜pol\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{pol}} denotes invocations of a post-trained policy, and adds to 𝒜Hinfo\mathcal{A}_{H}^{\mathrm{info}} a call that returns the annotated task demonstration on request. In each policy invocation, the agent specifies a step limit within which the post-trained policy executes autonomously under the fixed task instruction before returning an updated observation through 𝒪H\mathcal{O}_{H}. In this configuration, the agent alternates between issuing direct waypoint commands and invoking the post-trained policy for closed-loop trajectory execution, while retaining task planning, progress monitoring, and error recovery. Section 5 characterizes the capability boundary under direct control, and Section 6 evaluates how the harness with policy affects performance across capability dimensions.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Benchmark

EBench (Gao et al., 2026) is a diagnostic simulation benchmark for generalist robot manipulation, built on GenManip (Gao et al., 2025) and Isaac Sim with the ARX Lift 2 dual-arm mobile robot. Its 26 tasks span 9 scene categories across household, retail, and industrial settings, testing functional contexts such as food preparation, household cleaning, retail checkout, and component assembly. Completing these tasks requires relating object functions and spatial layouts to the task goal and sequencing the necessary manipulation steps. EBench annotates each task along five capability dimensions: scene, atomic skill, operating mode, manipulation precision, and task horizon. Our analyses mainly group tasks by the last three, and Appendix C.2 reports the results of Section 6 by atomic skill. Operating mode, which we refer to as mobility, separates 19 mobile from 7 tabletop tasks, manipulation precision separates 14 low-, 8 medium-, and 4 high-precision tasks, and task horizon separates 11 short- from 15 long-horizon tasks. The 510 test episodes span four generalization dimensions: Background with unseen backgrounds, Object with unseen object instances, Instruction with paraphrased instructions, and Mix with their joint perturbation.

The evaluation covers all 26 test tasks across 510 episodes, with 20 episodes for each of 24 tasks and 15 each for Sandwich and Microwave, spanning 468 distinct scenes. Performance is evaluated using two official metrics: task success rate (SR) and stage-completion score, which assigns partial credit for intermediate stages completed by the end of an episode according to task-specific rules. Both metrics are first averaged across episodes within each task and then averaged equally across all 26 tasks. Each episode is bounded by a task-specific physics-step limit ranging from 1,500 to 5,000 steps at 30 Hz, which is not disclosed to the agent.

4.2 Agent and Control Interface

We use GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026) with high reasoning effort as the core of the agent and initiate an independent session thread for each episode. At each decision step, based on the current visual and proprioceptive observations, the agent outputs one or more EEF and base waypoints, including target gripper states and execution durations. Meanwhile, the agent provides a brief text explaining the rationale for the command, which we refer to as its stated reason. These waypoints are interpolated into an action chunk and executed in the simulator, after which the updated observations are returned. The shared task prompt includes empirical operational routines, such as grasp verification: closing the gripper while stationary, lifting by 1 cm, and confirming that the object moves with the gripper, as detailed in Appendix A. Token usage, tool calls, and inference time are unconstrained. If the agent terminates an episode before the physics-step limit, the robot holds its final pose until the evaluation server computes the official SR and score.

Observation protocol.

Across both direct control and the harness with policy, the agent is evaluated under the same observation protocol as post-trained policies, receiving only RGB camera observations and proprioceptive robot states through pre-defined tools. Specifically, the interface supplies the views of three RGB cameras: the overview camera, termed overlook in the prompts, and the left and right wrist cameras. All three views are provided at the first step and can be requested selectively thereafter, together with the proprioceptive state comprising both EEF poses, gripper widths, the mobile base pose, and elapsed simulator steps. It provides no depth maps, camera calibration parameters, ground-truth object poses, segmentation masks, intermediate reward signals, subgoal indicators, or remaining step budgets. Official SR and score values are computed only after an episode terminates, and no state or experience is retained across episodes.

Annotated task demonstrations.

Each task is accompanied by a detailed task description derived from a single demonstration in the EBench training set as single-shot ICL. Specifically, prior to evaluation, a separate GPT-6-Astra instance with high reasoning effort inspects one training trajectory, selects 10–18 keyframes, summarizes the operation sequence, and pairs the selected keyframes with the recorded robot states and actions, as shown in Appendix A.3. During evaluation, the agent is instructed to adapt the demonstrated procedure and spatial relations to current visual observations rather than replaying recorded coordinates.

4.3 Configurations

We evaluate the GPT-6-Astra-based agent under two agent configurations, direct control and harness with policy instantiated with either π0.5\pi_{0.5} or InternW0-Δ\Delta, as illustrated in Figure 1.

Direct control.

The agent harness exposes only the EEF waypoint interface described above, and the agent invokes no external policy. This configuration isolates the standalone manipulation capability of the MLLM core.

Harness with policy.

In this configuration, the agent retains the EEF waypoint interface and can additionally invoke one of two frozen post-trained policies as a tool: the official leaderboard checkpoint of the VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a) or the WAM InternW0-Δ\Delta (Miao et al., 2026), both post-trained on EBench demonstrations. For each policy invocation, the agent specifies a step limit of 1–300 physics steps together with a stated reason. Within this step limit, the post-trained policy executes autonomously under the fixed task instruction, after which the updated visual and proprioceptive observations are returned to the agent. The harness also lets the agent query the annotated task demonstration again at any point. At each decision step, the agent chooses between issuing direct EEF waypoints and invoking the post-trained policy. In other words, the agent controls when and for how many steps the policy executes, but cannot pass agent-modified task prompts to the underlying policy, as discussed in Section 6.5.

4.4 Compared Policies

We compare the GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control and in the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} or InternW0-Δ\Delta against the post-trained VLA and WAM policies on the EBench leaderboard, as summarized in Table 1. Dimension-level and per-task analyses in Section 5 compare the agent against eight post-trained policies with per-task results on the 510 test episodes: OpenWAM-α\alpha (Wang et al., 2026b), InternW0-Δ\Delta (Miao et al., 2026), Qwen-RobotManip (Yuan et al., 2026a), π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a), InternVLA-A1.5 (Ma et al., 2026a), π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2025b), GigaBrain-0.7 (GigaBrain Team et al., 2026), and Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026b), all post-trained on the public EBench training set of 6,600 episodes across the 26 tasks. All comparisons across configurations of the agent are paired by test episode, with statistical procedures detailed in Appendix B.3.

5 Capability Boundary Under Direct Control

This section evaluates the GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control, in which the harness exposes observations and EEF waypoint commands but no post-trained policy. Every motion of the robot is therefore commanded by GPT-6-Astra itself, so the results isolate the manipulation capabilities of the MLLM. We first compare overall performance, task groups, and generalization dimensions with those of the eight post-trained policies, and then trace the failure patterns of unsuccessful episodes, the agent’s adaptation within an episode, and the safety risks of its execution. Through case studies and a pilot experiment, we further examine the role of the in-context demonstration and zero-shot compositional generalization, and finally summarize the resulting capability boundary.

5.1 Overall Performance

The GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control receives a single annotated demonstration per task and no parameter updates, yet it is competitive with VLA and WAM policies post-trained on 6,600 demonstrations of the same tasks. Compared with the eight post-trained policies in Table 1, the direct-control agent ranks third on both metrics with 46.7% SR and a 0.654 score. It trails only two WAMs, as OpenWAM-α\alpha reaches 55.3% SR and a 0.701 score and InternW0-Δ\Delta reaches 49.2% SR and a 0.660 score. It outperforms the remaining six policies, including the VLAs Qwen-RobotManip with 45.6% SR and a 0.608 score and π0.5\pi_{0.5} with 41.4% SR and a 0.544 score. Appendix Tables B.2 and B.3 report the per-task SR and score.

The gap between score and SR shows that the direct-control agent frequently earns stage credit in episodes that it does not finish. SR counts only complete successes, whereas the score also credits the stages completed before an unsuccessful episode ends. The SR of the direct-control agent trails that of InternW0-Δ\Delta by 2.5 percentage points and exceeds that of Qwen-RobotManip by only 1.1 points, whereas its score nearly matches that of InternW0-Δ\Delta and clearly exceeds those of Qwen-RobotManip and π0.5\pi_{0.5}. More generally, its score exceeds its SR by a larger margin than that of any post-trained policy. Section 5.2 therefore first uses Figure 2 to locate where the agent leads and trails, and Section 5.3 then examines the stages at which its episodes fail.

5.2 Capability Profile Across Task Groups and Generalization Dimensions

Across task groups, the performance of the direct-control agent splits by the type of demand rather than declining uniformly with task difficulty, as shown in Figures 2a and 3a and Appendix Figure B.2. It ranks first on short-horizon tasks and second on mobile and low-precision tasks, where only OpenWAM-α\alpha leads it. It drops to seventh on long-horizon and tabletop tasks and to eighth on high-precision tasks. The following paragraphs profile the agent along the horizon, mobility, and precision of the tasks and along the generalization dimensions, and Section 5.3 traces the failures behind the trailing ranks to their mechanisms.

Task horizon.

The horizon of a task separates the agent’s strongest group from one of its weakest. On the 11 short-horizon tasks, it achieves the highest SR of 73.2% and score of 0.766, surpassing all eight post-trained policies including OpenWAM-α\alpha at 65.9% SR and a 0.700 score. Eight of these 11 tasks require only low precision, and most of them consist of locating an object and its target, repositioning the base, and carrying the object between them, which the agent plans from its current views and executes with base and EEF waypoints. When a task reduces to such coarse transport between located targets, a single annotated demonstration and the priors of the MLLM therefore suffice for the agent to exceed policies post-trained on the full training set across this group. On the 15 long-horizon tasks, by contrast, the agent reaches only 27.3% SR, whereas OpenWAM-α\alpha reaches 47.6%. On these tasks, the agent often completes the early stages but not the full task. On Detergent, for example, it reaches a mean score of 0.80 but completes the full task in only 55% of episodes.

Mobility.

The mobility groups order task difficulty differently for the agent than for several post-trained policies. Because 10 of the 11 short-horizon tasks are mobile, the agent ranks second on the 19 mobile tasks with 56.6% SR. On the seven tabletop tasks, its SR falls to 20.0%, whereas Qwen-RobotManip reaches 50.0%. Qwen-RobotManip and GigaBrain-0.7, by contrast, achieve a higher SR on tabletop tasks than on mobile tasks. The tabletop gap extends beyond the four high-precision tabletop tasks to the other three: Frame, Flip cup & cookies, and Glass into box. On these three tasks, the agent reaches a mean SR of 31.7%, whereas Qwen-RobotManip reaches 91.7%. On the mobile tasks, in turn, the agent’s leading results rest on visual grounding. The Bookmark task requires locating a thin, flat bookmark on a desk crowded with visually similar stationery and everyday objects and placing it onto an open book. The agent succeeds in 90% of these episodes, whereas π0.5\pi_{0.5} reaches 55% and the remaining seven post-trained policies reach 25%–45%. In the Teacup & teapot task, the agent has to tell the two objects apart and place the teacup on the saucer and the teapot on the tray. It reaches 85% SR and a 0.93 score, whereas InternW0-Δ\Delta and Qwen-RobotManip lead the post-trained policies with 45% SR. In the Remote task, the agent must place the remote into a designated compartment of a divided holder. It succeeds in every episode, whereas InternW0-Δ\Delta succeeds in 85%. Perfume also targets a compartment of a divided organizer, and on this task the agent ties OpenWAM-α\alpha for the highest SR at 75% with a higher score of 0.88 against 0.78. Bookmark, Teacup & teapot, and Remote are the three tasks on which the agent leads all eight post-trained policies. These three tasks and Perfume all require locating the specified object among distractors or the specified compartment among several before placing the object there. These leads therefore indicate that the agent grounds objects and targets reliably, as Appendix Figure D.1 illustrates for Bookmark and Remote from the grasp approach to the placement.

Manipulation precision.

Success declines most steeply with the precision that a task demands. The SR of the agent falls from 60.6% on low-precision tasks to 40.2% on medium-precision tasks and 11.3% on high-precision tasks. Its rank drops accordingly from second to fourth and eighth. On high-precision tasks, OpenWAM-α\alpha and π0.5\pi_{0.5} retain 32.5% and 17.5%, respectively. On Peg in hole and Tighten nut, the agent reaches SRs of only 20% and 10% yet mean scores of 0.60 and 0.55. Every unsuccessful episode on these tasks earns 0.50 for positioning the part at the target location and then fails at the final insertion or threading step, as shown in Appendix Figure D.3. The agent’s failures on these two tasks thus concentrate on the final contact step.

Generalization dimensions.

Across the generalization dimensions, the agent’s strength holds even with minimal task context. The post-trained policies are trained on 6,600 episodes, whereas the direct-control agent receives for each task only one annotated demonstration derived from a single training episode. This demonstration cannot fully illustrate the shifts that the test episodes apply along the four dimensions of Object, Background, Instruction, and Mix. Even so, the SR of the direct-control agent stays between 44.2% and 50.8% across the four dimensions, as shown in Figure 2b and Appendix Table B.4. This 6.6-point range is the smallest among the agent and the eight post-trained policies. The four policies in Figure 2b vary more widely: 7.7 points for InternW0-Δ\Delta, 11.5 points for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, 16.9 points for OpenWAM-α\alpha, and 21.5 points for Qwen-RobotManip. What the agent takes from the demonstration therefore transfers across these shifts. Moreover, the advantage grows under the Mix dimension, where the object instance, background texture, and instruction phrasing change jointly. Every post-trained policy reaches its lowest SR under Mix. OpenWAM-α\alpha, for example, falls from 61.5% under Background to 44.6% under Mix, and Qwen-RobotManip falls from 55.4% to 33.8%. The direct-control agent, by contrast, maintains 46.2% SR and a 0.643 score under Mix and ranks first on both metrics. In conclusion, the generalization shifts limit the post-trained policies more than the direct-control agent. The limits of the agent lie instead in the manipulation demands of the long-horizon, tabletop, and high-precision groups, which the next subsection examines.

5.3 Failure Patterns and Token Cost

Most unsuccessful episodes of the direct-control agent end with partial progress rather than failing initially, which explains the score margin of Section 5.1. Of the 510 episodes, 237 end in complete success, and 188 of the 273 unsuccessful episodes achieve a nonzero score, so only 85 end at zero, as shown in Figure 3b. Zero scores concentrate on Gear, Utensils, and Glass into box, where the agent fails before any scored progress in 75%, 65%, and 50% of episodes, respectively. The trajectory analysis below traces the unsuccessful episodes to four mechanisms: imprecise contact geometry, delayed feedback over long horizons, uncoordinated bimanual motion, and unconfirmed completion claims. A final paragraph measures the token cost of the resulting failures.

Contact geometry at the final step.

Precise contact fails where the agent has to infer geometry from images. The agent does not infer the surface height, part clearance, and contact geometry precisely enough for the final insertion and threading from RGB views and the base-relative EEF pose alone. Post-trained policies receive the same RGB views without depth but map them to contact motions learned from demonstration trajectories. The same limit appears on tasks with moderate nominal precision. On Glass into box, closing the case requires folding both temples inward, but the agent’s corrective pushes leave a temple protruding and prevent the lid from closing, as shown in Appendix Figure D.6b.

Delayed feedback and cascading disturbances over long horizons.

The rollouts of long-horizon tasks point to two causes of failure. First, the agent detects disturbances late and recovers from them slowly. It receives an observation only after each commanded waypoint chunk finishes. Although 84% of its motion commands consist of a single waypoint, each command runs for a median of 48 physics steps, whereas π0.5\pi_{0.5} and InternW0-Δ\Delta replan every 30 and 10 physics steps, as Section 6.1 describes. A grasp loss or contact change within a chunk therefore persists until the chunk returns, and the retries that follow consume the remaining physics steps. As a result, the step limit ends 229 of all 273 unsuccessful episodes and is by far their most common ending. Second, the agent plans its approaches and grasps without anticipating how contact will move the object, so the scene becomes unstable over a long task. On Detergent, a bottle tips over or falls during the agent’s own approach, grasp, or transport in 19 of the 20 episodes, and on Bottle this happens in 11 of the 20. The agent must then grasp the fallen bottle again from the table. In one Detergent episode, for example, the agent places the first of three bottles within 11 commands, but the second bottle falls during the next command, which withdraws and approaches over 100 physics steps. The agent spends the remaining 92 commands grasping that bottle again and then the third bottle, which slips during transport. The episode reaches the step limit with two bottles placed. Such cascades accumulate most on Bottle, which is one of the two longest tasks. No evaluated policy or configuration completes Bottle, as analyzed in Section 6.6.

Uncoordinated bimanual motion.

On bimanual tasks, the agent coordinates its two arms only between waypoint chunks. Each chunk executes open loop, so the agent cannot adjust one arm to the contact that the other arm makes during execution, and one hand can withdraw or move before the other has secured the shared object. On Flip cup & cookies, where the cup passes from one hand to the other, the agent fails in 90% of episodes. Appendix Figure D.3c shows one such episode, in which the supporting hand withdraws during the second handover and the cup falls off the table. On Frame, the agent takes the division of labor between the arms from the demonstration, as analyzed in Section 5.6. Its SR of 65% on this task exceeds the 50% of OpenWAM-α\alpha but stays below the 95% of Qwen-RobotManip.

Unconfirmed completion claims.

Finally, the direct-control agent sometimes ends an episode early because it misjudges completion. The agent ends 43 unsuccessful episodes before the step limit, and 21 of them end with a claim of task success while a subgoal remains unmet. Seven of these claims come from Dishwasher, and the agent makes all seven with the door still open, as shown in Appendix Figure D.5. The instruction of this task asks to put every bowl into the dishwasher, and the last keyframe of the demonstration shows the door closed, yet the agent treats the placement of both bowls as completion. It states an intent to close the door after loading in only one of the 20 episodes, which is also its only success.

Token cost of failures and long horizons.

These failures also dominate the token cost of direct control. The agent resends its growing episode context with every call, so the tokens of an episode grow with its number of calls, as detailed in Appendix C.3. Across the 510 episodes, the Pearson correlation between the two is r=0.88r=0.88. An unsuccessful episode keeps issuing corrections until it reaches the step limit or ends early. On average, it consumes 5.45M tokens over 55.9 calls, roughly three times the 1.84M tokens and twice the 27.4 calls of a successful episode. Long horizons compound this cost, as an episode of a long-horizon task consumes 5.40M tokens against 1.63M on a short-horizon task while succeeding less often. One success on a long-horizon task therefore costs 20.6M tokens when the tokens spent on unsuccessful episodes within each group are included. This cost is about nine times the 2.23M tokens per success on a short-horizon task.

5.4 Adaptive Capabilities

The direct-control agent observes the scene only between its own action chunks, yet the returned observations give it in-episode feedback that informs its next decision. After a failed action, the agent records a possible explanation, explores the workspace, and revises its approach. Such in-episode diagnosis is frequent across the 510 episodes: the agent’s stated reasons name a slip, a drop, or a displaced object in 302 of them, as detailed in Appendix B.2. The two examples in Figure 4 show two forms of this adaptation.

First, the agent diagnoses failures that occur while a chunk executes and changes its motion strategy accordingly. For example, in the Apple to bowl task of Figure 4a, the interface reports no failure when the apple slips, but the agent infers a possible slip from the closed finger gap and withdraws to obtain a wider view. After regrasping the apple, it avoids the base motion that preceded the slip, transports the apple with the arm alone, and completes the episode. Second, the agent adjusts the contact geometry with the physical guidance supplied in its prompt. In the Coffee beans task of Figure 4b, an initial sweep leaves the beans in place. The agent then applies a supplied caveat that the measured local EEF zz-coordinate is not the height above the tabletop, repeats the sweep 25 mm lower, and tilts the fingertips downward to establish contact with the surface.

The two episodes thus separate the agent’s diagnosis and adaptation from the precision of its physical execution. In both, the agent states a likely cause of the failure and revises its strategy, and the outcome then depends on how precisely the revised motion makes contact. In the Apple to bowl episode, the revised transport completes the task. In the Coffee beans episode, the lowered and tilted sweep follows the supplied caveat quoted in Appendix D.1, yet the episode ends at a 0.50 score with the collection incomplete. In-episode adaptation therefore reaches the level of diagnosis and strategy, while fine contact marks the boundary that Section 5.8 locates.

5.5 Safety in Execution

Aggregate task scores do not capture how safely the agent executes its commands, and here the direct-control agent shows clear weaknesses. They stem mainly from unconstrained execution, as the agent drives each command toward its target without accounting for the other arm, the workspace bounds, contact with the scene, or the speed of the motion. Grip losses are common, and more than half of them occur outside grasp tests. Across the 510 episodes under direct control, the gripper-state criteria of Appendix B.2 identify 811 grip losses in 333 episodes. Of these losses, 469 in 265 episodes occur in calls whose stated reasons describe no test of a grasp. Recurring patterns in the recorded rollouts illustrate four resulting hazards, and Appendix Figure D.4 shows the first three. First, independent single-arm commands can destabilize held objects during bimanual tasks. In the Dishwasher task, for example, a bowl slips from the left gripper while the right hand opens the door, as shown in Appendix Figure D.4a. Second, recovery attempts can drive the robot beyond safe workspace bounds. After an apple falls outside the workspace, for example, the agent keeps requesting EEF targets beneath the table and behind the robot base, as in Appendix Figure D.4b. Third, height and contact with the scene are hard to judge from RGB images without depth. On Coffee beans, a held jar and later the spoon strike the table edge in an awkward pose, while sweeping motions elsewhere pass above the surface, as in Appendix Figure D.4c.

The fourth hazard concerns the speed of wrist and joint motion. The agent commands target EEF poses directly and relies on the inverse-kinematics solver to compute joint trajectories, so its commands can turn the wrist through large angles within a few physics steps. In 31 of the 510 episodes, a wrist turns through 90∘ or more within 24 physics steps, and a joint exceeds 0.08 rad per physics step in 169 episodes. By comparison, the segments that π0.5\pi_{0.5} executes in the harness with policy of Section 6 contain no wrist turn this large within 24 physics steps, and they exceed the joint threshold in only 59 episodes, as detailed in Appendix B.2. On physical hardware, the forces and torques that these fast rotations require risk motor damage or collisions. Together, these cases highlight the need to preserve grasp stability, enforce workspace and motion constraints, and account for contact throughout manipulation before real-world deployment.

5.6 Case Studies: In-Context Learning, Adaptation, and Precision

In-context learning.

On Frame and Gear, the annotated demonstration conveys task-level structure to the direct-control agent but not the precise action of a final contact step. Appendix D.3 compares runs with and without the demonstration on all 20 test episodes of each task. On Frame, the demonstration raises the number of successful episodes from 1/20 to 13/20 and the mean score from 0.283 to 0.800, because it supplies the two-arm division of labor that zero-shot execution does not find. On Gear, by contrast, both conditions reach 3/20 successes and a mean score of 0.200, although the failures differ. Without the demonstration, the agent leaves the gear outside the assembly region. With it, the agent positions the gear between the mounted gears and lowers it, yet 15 of the 20 episodes still end without a scored stage, so the mean score does not rise above the zero-shot level.

Adaptation and precision.

On two contrasting tasks, the direct-control agent adjusts its grasps and revisits disrupted goals, whereas the post-trained policies execute precise manipulation more accurately. Appendix D.2 sets the agent beside π0.5\pi_{0.5} and OpenWAM-α\alpha on Teacup & teapot, where it leads, and on Glass into box, where it trails. On Teacup & teapot, the agent targets the handle region and adjusts its wrist and gripper configuration across attempts. When later manipulation displaces the cup from the saucer, it revisits the cup and carries it back toward the saucer. In contrast, π0.5\pi_{0.5} repeats approach and retraction motions without completing the cup transfer, and OpenWAM-α\alpha moves the teapot onto the tray while the cup stays off the saucer. On Glass into box, however, both post-trained policies fold the temples and OpenWAM-α\alpha also closes the lid, whereas the agent’s corrective contacts leave a temple protruding as described in Section 5.3.

5.7 Compositional Generalization

To evaluate whether the direct-control agent and post-trained policies can compose skills into a new multi-step sequence, we conduct a pilot experiment with an instruction outside the standard EBench task set: placing a bookmark and then a pen onto the same open book, as shown in Figure 5. The EBench training set contains placing a bookmark onto a book and placing a pen into a holder or onto a ruler, but not placing a pen onto a book. This setting therefore tests more than the sequencing of two familiar tasks, as the combined objective includes a subtask absent from the robot-policy training data. Completing the first placement in the prescribed order awards a partial score of 0.50. The agent and both post-trained policies each run 10 rollouts, and the agent runs zero-shot without an in-context demonstration. It succeeds in all 10 episodes with a 1.00 mean score by placing the bookmark and then the pen onto the book in the required order. By contrast, π0.5\pi_{0.5} and OpenWAM-α\alpha achieve 0/10 successes with mean scores of 0.40 and 0.35, respectively. In their rollouts, both post-trained policies either place the bookmark and stop without initiating the second step or directly manipulate the pen out of order. In this pilot, generalization to individual atomic skills does not yield multi-step compositional execution, whereas the agent’s zero-shot instruction following completes the sequence.

5.8 The Capability Boundary

Taken together, the results of this section place the capability boundary of the direct-control agent at the transition from task-level reasoning to physical execution, and the way in which the agent acts explains why the boundary lies there. On the reasoning side, the semantic and spatial priors of multimodal pretraining supply the task-level knowledge, so that one annotated demonstration per task suffices to direct them. On the execution side, the agent acts through EEF waypoint chunks and observes the scene only after each chunk, so it lacks the continuous physical feedback that precise contact, coordinated two-arm motion, and long horizons require. The post-trained policies learn their control from demonstration trajectories and act on fresh observations throughout execution, so they receive this feedback by design.

6 Harness with Policy

This section tests whether combining the agent with post-trained policies can overcome the execution bottlenecks of direct control. We build the harness-with-policy setting following the Harness VLA framework (Zhang et al., 2026b) and evaluate it across all 510 EBench test episodes with two representative policies: the VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a) and the WAM InternW0-Δ\Delta (Miao et al., 2026). We first describe the harness design and compare the two harness configurations with direct control and the standalone policies in overall performance, across task groups, and across generalization dimensions. We then diagnose how failure patterns shift once the agent invokes a policy, analyze its policy invocation behavior, and finally examine the failure modes shared across both policies to identify the sources of the remaining gap. The final subsection also compares the token cost of each configuration.

6.1 Harness Design

Following Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b), our harness with policy exposes a frozen post-trained policy as a callable tool alongside the direct EEF interface described in Section 4.3, together with a call that returns the annotated task demonstration on request. In each invocation, the agent assigns 1–300 physics steps. Within these steps, the policy acts without intervention from the agent and then returns new visual and proprioceptive observations to the agent. Both harness configurations keep the system prompt, annotated task demonstration, and test scenes fixed and differ in the policy and its execution and history settings. The two policies contrast in temporal conditioning and in standalone strength. For the VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a), the harness uses the official EBench leaderboard checkpoint. This policy acts on the current observation alone, predicts 50 joint and gripper targets per inference, and replans every 30 physics steps. Evaluated alone, it trails the direct-control agent on both metrics in Table 1. The WAM InternW0-Δ\Delta (Miao et al., 2026) is likewise post-trained on EBench demonstrations but additionally conditions on two earlier frames of the episode. It predicts 32 joint, gripper, and base targets per inference and replans every 10 physics steps, which is three times as often as π0.5\pi_{0.5}, as detailed in Appendix C. Alone, it exceeds direct control on both metrics. Pairing the same agent with both policies therefore asks whether the agent still gains from a policy weaker than itself and whether a policy stronger than the agent lifts the combination beyond both components.

6.2 Overall Performance

Each harness configuration outperforms both of its standalone components in Table 2, though the gains are asymmetric: pairing with the stronger policy yields the higher overall performance, whereas the weaker policy gains more from the agent. Relative to the agent under direct control, overall SR rises by 6.3 percentage points to 53.0% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and by 9.3 points to 56.0% with InternW0-Δ\Delta. The score rises from 0.654 to 0.692 and 0.744, respectively. OpenWAM-α\alpha is the strongest of the eight post-trained policies, and the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta surpasses it on both metrics and ranks first in Table 1. The harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} trails only OpenWAM-α\alpha among these eight. Relative to each policy alone, by contrast, SR rises by 11.6 points with π0.5\pi_{0.5} but only by 6.8 points with InternW0-Δ\Delta. Appendix Table C.1 reports the per-task results.

These net improvements combine resolved failures with newly failed episodes. Across the 510 paired episodes, the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeeds on 91 episodes that fail under direct control and fails on 59 that succeed under it. The harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta gains 96 episodes and loses 49, as Appendix Table C.2 details. Figure 6 shows where this combination holds across task demands. On six of the seven task groups, each harness configuration comes within three percentage points of the stronger of its two components or exceeds it, whereas on high-precision tasks both configurations remain below the standalone policies. Section 6.3 traces these group results to individual tasks and generalization dimensions, and Section 6.4 then analyzes the episode-level failure patterns behind both.

6.3 Capability Profile Across Task Groups and Generalization Dimensions

Task groups.

The harness with policy improves task success mainly on long-horizon and tabletop tasks, where the post-trained policy outperforms the agent under direct control, and it keeps the agent’s lead on short-horizon tasks. With either policy, SR increases by roughly 13 percentage points on long-horizon tasks and by 11–14 percentage points on tabletop tasks in Table 2. These are two of the three groups on which the agent ranks lowest under direct control in Section 5.2. On these groups, invoking the policy brings the agent to about the level of the policy alone. Specifically, the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta matches InternW0-Δ\Delta alone on tabletop tasks at 33.6% and stays close to it on long-horizon tasks at 40.4% versus 42.0%. The harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} exceeds π0.5\pi_{0.5} alone on both groups, with 40.2% versus 33.4% on long-horizon tasks and 31.4% versus 29.3% on tabletop tasks. On short-horizon tasks, the agent already leads all compared post-trained policies under direct control. Both harness configurations preserve this strong performance and therefore outperform the corresponding policy alone by 18.2 percentage points. On Apple from shelf, for instance, InternW0-Δ\Delta alone achieves 15% SR, whereas the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta reaches 75% SR. Appendix B.3 details the statistical significance of task-level improvements across all 26 tasks.

Task-level gains on bimanual and articulated stages.

At the task level, the two largest gains over direct control arise with either policy on Glass into box and Dishwasher, as shown in Figure 7. On Glass into box, SR increases from 20% under direct control to 85% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 80% with InternW0-Δ\Delta. On Dishwasher, it increases from 5% to 60% and 75%, respectively. On these two tasks, the invoked policy executes the bimanual transport, temple folding, lid closure, and rack manipulation. These include the stages where the agent under direct control ran out of steps or ended early, as Appendix Figure E.2a,b illustrates for Glass into box.

Task-level shortfalls against either component.

Two sets of tasks depart from these gains. First, both harness configurations fall below direct control on four of the 11 tasks where neither policy alone exceeds the SR of direct control: Peg in hole, Pen, Microwave, and Teacup & teapot. On Peg in hole, for example, SR drops from 20% to 5% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 0% with InternW0-Δ\Delta, and on Pen from 15% to 5% and 0%. Second, the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta falls furthest below InternW0-Δ\Delta alone on Shop and Detergent, where SR drops from 60% to 5% and from 95% to 70%. On both tasks, InternW0-Δ\Delta executes more than 80% of the physics steps in the harness, so the policy itself performs most of the motion. The shortfall arises from objects lost during the delegated segments or after the agent resumes control. Section 6.4 traces both sets to their failure patterns.

Generalization dimensions.

The choice of policy also determines whether the harness keeps the balanced generalization profile of the agent under direct control, as shown in Figure 6b and d. With π0.5\pi_{0.5}, the harness stays above π0.5\pi_{0.5} alone on all four dimensions. Over direct control, however, it improves only on Object, where SR rises from 44.2% to 59.2%, and on Instruction, where it rises from 44.6% to 56.2%. On Background and Mix, it remains at about the level of direct control. As a result, its range across dimensions widens from 6.6 to 13.0 points. The newly failed episodes explain this pattern. Resolved failures are distributed evenly at 21 to 25 episodes per dimension. Newly failed episodes, by contrast, concentrate on Background and Mix with 22 and 21 episodes, against only 7 on Object and 9 on Instruction. By failure cause, 25 of these 43 newly failed episodes begin when the agent’s own grasp slips. By task, 21 of the 43 come from just four tasks. Teacup & teapot leads them, as all five of its Background episodes newly fail. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, newly failed episodes are fewer and spread more evenly at 9 to 17 per dimension, against 22 to 26 resolved failures on each. The harness therefore gains on every dimension and surpasses both of its components on each. Its Mix SR of 53.1% and score of 0.718 are the highest of all compared policies and configurations, and its range narrows to 4.6 points, the smallest in Appendix Table B.4.

6.4 Failures Resolved and Introduced by the Policy

Table 3 follows how the 510 episodes end under direct control and in each harness configuration. Most unsuccessful episodes reach the physics-step limit in all three configurations, and nearly all of the rest end early with an unconfirmed completion claim or a reported failure of the agent. This section compares each ending between direct control and the harness to show which failures the policy resolves and which it introduces. Section 6.6 then examines the episodes that fail with both policies.

Step-limit failures.

Invoking a policy mainly reduces failures at the step limit on long-horizon tasks but rarely resolves those on high-precision tasks, where both policies alone also remain weak. Relative to direct control, unsuccessful episodes that exhaust the physics-step limit decrease from 229 to 201 with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and to 178 with InternW0-Δ\Delta, and zero-score episodes decrease from 85 to 79 and 58, respectively. Of the 229 step-limit failures under direct control, 72 succeed with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 76 with InternW0-Δ\Delta, and most of these conversions occur on long-horizon tasks. On high-precision tasks, only 2 and 8 of the 59 step-limit failures succeed, as detailed in Appendix Table C.2. In the newly successful episodes, the policy executes 78% of the physics steps and typically completes the final stage itself, as it does in every newly successful episode of Dishwasher.

Unconfirmed completion claims.

Invoking a policy also reduces early terminations on an unconfirmed claim of completion from 21 under direct control to 15 with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 13 with InternW0-Δ\Delta. Of these 21 episodes, 10 and 11 become full successes in Appendix Table C.2. The policy brings this gain through execution. In 7 of the 10 and 8 of the 11 converted episodes, the last motion is a policy segment that completes the task, and every converted Dishwasher episode ends this way. The remaining claims concentrate on two tasks. Dishwasher accounts for 6 of the 15 claims with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and Gear accounts for 7 of the 13 with InternW0-Δ\Delta, whereas direct control makes a single claim on Gear. In these Gear episodes, the agent claims completion while the gear rests unseated near the middle shaft.

Object losses in newly failed episodes.

Object losses, by contrast, end more episodes in the harness configurations. In a grip loss, an object slips from a gripper that remains commanded closed and the fingers close fully, as detected by the criteria of Appendix B.2. Early terminations in which the agent reports an unrecoverable failure rise from 22 under direct control to 24 with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 33 with InternW0-Δ\Delta, and every one of them in either harness configuration names a lost object. Across the test set, 59 episodes that succeed under direct control newly fail in the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and 49 newly fail with InternW0-Δ\Delta. A call-by-call reading of these episodes shows that the two configurations lose objects in different ways, as reported in Appendix Table C.3. With π0.5\pi_{0.5}, 30 of the 59 begin with a slip of the agent’s own grasp during a lift test or transport. In the Teacup & teapot episode of Appendix Figure E.1c, for example, segments of π0.5\pi_{0.5} end with an empty hand before the agent’s own grasp of the teapot slips. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, 30 of the 49 lose or misplace an object during a policy segment or just after control returns to the agent. Shop leaves little margin for such a loss, as InternW0-Δ\Delta alone needs 4,161 to 4,876 of the 5,000 physics steps in its successful episodes. In the harness, the agent delegates more than three quarters of the physics steps in 17 of the 19 unsuccessful episodes, and the delegated segments include failed bimanual handovers and their retries. All 19 episodes end at the step limit, and the harness completes a single Shop episode. Across the four high-precision tasks, none of their 6 and 7 newly failed episodes completes the final contact stage. In these episodes, pegs slip or are released before seating, the nut is released unseated, and gears are released off-axis or not fully seated.

Unmaintained grasps after policy segments.

Policy segments hold objects more securely than the agent’s own commands. Within policy segments, grip losses occur 0.63 and 0.72 times per 1,000 held arm-steps with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and InternW0-Δ\Delta. Under the agent’s commands, they occur 2.18 and 2.22 times overall and 0.87 and 1.00 times outside its grasp tests, as detailed in Appendix C.2. The losses after a segment arise once control returns to the agent. The harness then holds each gripper at its measured finger width, and the agent receives fresh images together with these widths. Its next command, however, often operates one arm and leaves the holding arm unspecified instead of commanding it to stay closed. Counted per holding arm, such unmaintained grasps occur 338 times after a segment of π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 316 times after one of InternW0-Δ\Delta. A grip loss on that arm or a disruption reported in the agent’s next stated reasons follows within two calls in 17% and 19% of these cases, respectively, compared with 6.5% and 9.9% when the agent leaves a holding arm unspecified after one of its own commands in the same harness configuration. Stratified by task, the odds of such a disruption after a policy segment are 2.95 and 1.29 times those after the agent’s own commands, as detailed in Appendix C. All four Detergent episodes that newly fail in the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta are lost this way, as illustrated in Appendix E.3. The agent thus does not yet use the returned proprioceptive state to confirm and maintain a grasp that the policy has established.

6.5 Policy Invocation Behavior

Delegation over an episode.

The agent delegates first and takes control back as the episode proceeds. Successful episodes then return control to the policy, whereas unsuccessful ones stay largely under the agent’s own commands. In all 510 episodes with either policy, its first motion command is a policy invocation, and the policy executes 92–97% of the physics steps in the first tenth of an episode, as shown in Figure 8a. This share declines over the first half as the agent steps in with grasp tests, corrections, and recoveries. In the second half of successful episodes, the policy’s share recovers to 58–64% in the final tenth. Within the same task, successful episodes also leave about 14 points more of their steps to π0.5\pi_{0.5} than unsuccessful ones, and about 13 points more to InternW0-Δ\Delta. In unsuccessful episodes, by contrast, the policy’s share keeps falling to 35–36%, and 68% and 72% of these episodes end with a motion command of the agent. Unsuccessful episodes are also longer and contain more transitions between the agent and the policy. They average 7.2 transitions against 4.2 in successful episodes with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 6.8 against 3.8 with InternW0-Δ\Delta. Between transitions, however, the agent keeps control for longer stretches, with 0.26 and 0.24 transitions per motion command against 0.33 and 0.28 in successful episodes, as listed in Appendix Table C.5. The policy invocations of unsuccessful episodes also ask for recovery more often. With π0.5\pi_{0.5} and InternW0-Δ\Delta, 22.0% and 20.7% of these invocations are coded as asking the policy to recover a slipped, missed, or displaced object. These shares are more than three times the 6.3% and 5.8% in successful episodes in Table 3. Recovery requests thus mark the least successful episodes. Among the episodes with a reported disruption, those with a recovery request fail in 79.3% and 79.0% of cases, against 58.3% and 53.8% of those without one. The agent delegates 35% and 34% of the motion commands whose stated reasons report a slip, a lost object, or another disruption, and it executes the rest itself.

Competence and delegation across tasks.

Across tasks, the gain of the harness follows the competence of the policy, but the agent’s delegation does not. On the one hand, the change in SR from direct control tracks the advantage of the policy alone over the agent under direct control, with Pearson correlations of r=0.77r=0.77 for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and r=0.68r=0.68 for InternW0-Δ\Delta, as shown in Figure 8b. On the other hand, the policy executes on average 66.9% of the physics steps of a task with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 65.4% with InternW0-Δ\Delta. This share is not significantly correlated with the SR of the policy alone, with r=0.31r=0.31 and r=0.23r=0.23 in Figure 8c. For example, π0.5\pi_{0.5} alone succeeds in at most 10% of episodes on seven tasks, yet the agent still leaves it 60% of the physics steps on these tasks on average and 42–90% per task. The share is 71% on the 11 tasks on which π0.5\pi_{0.5} alone succeeds in at least half of the episodes. By the same thresholds, InternW0-Δ\Delta is weak on five tasks and strong on 15, and the agent leaves it 68% and 71% of the physics steps on them. The share differs instead by horizon. With π0.5\pi_{0.5} and InternW0-Δ\Delta, it is 58% and 54% on short-horizon tasks against 73% and 74% on long-horizon tasks.

Subgoal delegation under a fixed task instruction.

The agent’s stated reasons show that it divides the work with the policy by subgoal, whereas the policy pursues the whole task. In a successful Flip cup & cookies episode, for instance, the agent tests a grasp with its own waypoints under the stated reason “Test cup grasp by raising 1 cm without rotation”. It then leaves the handover, the reorientation of the cup, and the pour to InternW0-Δ\Delta, as listed in Appendix E.1. In a Gear episode with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, the agent assigns each invocation a stage, from carrying the gear to the middle mounting position to its fine alignment and seating. At times it also assigns a verification such as “Verify the released blue gear remains seated while withdrawing the hand”. The policy, however, is conditioned on the task instruction instead of that stage and reports nothing back. The agent then claims completion after checking only the overview image while the gear rests on the board unseated, as detailed in Appendix E.2. These episodes show that the agent’s subgoal does not reach the policy upon invocation.

6.6 Failure Modes Shared Across Policies

The two harness configurations fail largely on the same tasks. Of the 510 test episodes, 164 fail with both policies. This count is close to the 168 expected if the two configurations failed independently within each task. On the four high-precision tasks, 65 of the 80 episodes fail with both. Shared failures are therefore governed by task-level difficulty rather than by scene-specific factors.

Within these shared failures, however, where an episode breaks along its chain of grasping, transfer, and contact depends on the policy. The two runs of an episode end with the same category of decisive incident in only 58 of the 164 episodes, as broken down in Appendix Table C.4. First, object losses decide 109 shared failures with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 105 with InternW0-Δ\Delta, and their location shifts with the policy. With π0.5\pi_{0.5}, 58 of these losses occur during the agent’s own lift tests and transport and 37 inside policy segments. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, the order reverses, as 53 occur inside policy segments and 42 during the agent’s own lift tests and transport. The remaining 14 and 10 follow a grasp left unmaintained after a policy segment, as analyzed in Section 6.4. Second, 19 and 24 shared failures stall at the final insertion, threading, or seating stage, and 16 and 15 spend policy segments empty-handed or on the wrong object. Third, 19 and 20 shared failures end without a single decisive object loss. Of these, 16 and 11 reach the step limit as recovered slips, empty grasps, and displaced objects accumulate. Bottle accounts for 14 of these 27 step-limit runs, and in 11 of the 14, bottles slip, fall beside or behind the basket, or lie outside it. No run on Bottle places more than 9 of the 12 bottles. The other 3 and 9 end with a false completion claim.

6.7 Shifted Boundary, Remaining Gaps, and Token Cost

The harness with policy moves the boundary of Section 5.8 where the policy supplies the closed-loop execution that direct control lacks, chiefly on the long-horizon and tabletop tasks. Two limits remain, and a final paragraph examines how the shift changes the agent’s token cost.

Shared ceiling on high-precision contact.

First, the agent and both policies share an execution ceiling on high-precision contact, so combining them does not lift it. A per-task choice in hindsight between the agent alone and the policy alone reaches only 21.3% SR on the high-precision tasks with either policy. The best of all three components reaches 30.0%, which remains below the 32.5% of OpenWAM-α\alpha.

Gap to the better component from loose coordination.

Second, the combination loses part of what its components achieve alone. The per-task choice of the better component would attain 56.2% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 60.8% with InternW0-Δ\Delta. It would thus exceed the respective harness configuration by 3.1 and 4.8 points over all tasks and by 13.8 and 8.8 points on the high-precision tasks. The harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} exceeds both of its components on only ten tasks and falls below the better one on thirteen. The harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta exceeds both on eight tasks and falls below the better one on eleven. The preceding analyses trace this loss to three sources in how agent and policy coordinate. First, the agent allocates physics steps to the policy by task horizon rather than by the policy’s competence on the task, as shown in Section 6.5. Second, each policy segment conditions on the task instruction and the observations listed in Section 6.1 rather than on the agent’s subgoal or the stages already completed, as shown in Section 6.5. Third, once a policy segment ends, the agent does not command the holding arm to stay closed at the returned finger width, as shown in Section 6.4.

Token cost.

Invoking a policy also moves computation from the agent into the policy. The agent consumes 1.83M tokens per episode with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 2.22M with InternW0-Δ\Delta, which is 52% and 41% less than the 3.77M under direct control. It also makes 23.7 and 22.7 tool calls per episode instead of 42.6. Per success, it needs 3.5M and 4.0M tokens, which is 57% and 51% fewer than the 8.1M under direct control. The savings concentrate where direct control is most expensive, as shown in Figure 9. On long-horizon tasks, one success costs 6.2M and 7.5M tokens in the two harness configurations, which is less than two fifths of its cost under direct control. On short-horizon tasks, the cost per success falls by only a quarter to a third. Within each configuration, unsuccessful episodes still consume 2.6 and 2.4 times the tokens of successful ones, because tokens grow with the number of calls in the harness as well. At the published tariff of GPT-6-Astra, the agent’s tokens cost USD 16.82 per success under direct control but only 4.99 and 5.49 in the two harness configurations, as detailed in Appendix C.3. In exchange, the policy adds 45 inferences of π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 135 of InternW0-Δ\Delta per episode.

7 Conclusions and Future Directions

This report profiles GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness. The agent observes the scene under the same visual and proprioceptive protocol as post-trained policies and acts first under direct control and then in a harness with a post-trained VLA or WAM. Under direct control, the capability boundary of the agent lies between flexible task interpretation and reliable physical execution. Without robot-specific post-training of the MLLM, the direct-control agent draws on multimodal pretraining and one annotated demonstration for each task to compete with post-trained policies overall, with particular strengths in visual grounding, robustness to generalization shifts, adaptation to failures during an episode, and zero-shot composition of skills. Physical execution, by contrast, exposes a tension in how the agent controls the robot. The agent chooses its corrections between waypoint chunks, whereas grasps, contacts, and the alignment of parts evolve within each chunk, so precise contact, bimanual coordination, and long horizons limit its success. Because each correction also resends the accumulated context, the unsuccessful and long-horizon episodes that this tension produces account for most of the agent’s token cost. The same unconstrained execution also drops held objects outside the agent’s deliberate grasp tests and at times produces abrupt wrist rotations that risk damaging physical hardware.

Invoking a post-trained policy moves part of this boundary. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, the harness with policy reaches the highest SR and score in Table 1, and with either policy the agent needs far fewer tokens per success on long-horizon tasks, where direct control is costliest. However, two shortfalls of the combination indicate where further progress is needed. First, precise contact limits the agent and each policy alike, so combining them leaves this ceiling in place. Second, the combination falls short of its better component on many tasks, because the coordination between agent and policy remains loose. The agent delegates without regard to the policy’s competence, the policy pursues the task instruction rather than the agent’s subgoal, and when control returns from the policy, the agent often leaves the holding arm unmaintained, allowing grasped objects to slip. These limitations motivate us to explore several directions.

Designing subtask interfaces and training policies as learnable tools.

In the evaluated harness, the agent passes the policy only a step count, so it decides when the policy acts but can neither assign a subgoal nor receive a report of its completion. A finer interface would not only expose learned skills as tools that a planner selects (RLinf, 2026) but also pass an explicit subgoal to the policy, verify the entry and exit conditions of each subtask (Xu et al., 2026), and return whether the subgoal was reached. Such an interface also requires a policy that can serve it. The evaluated policies are post-trained on complete EBench task trajectories under the task instruction, whereas the harness invokes them mid-episode from states that the agent has reached and for subgoals that the agent has chosen. The policy itself therefore has to be trained as a learnable tool of the harness. This training spans three levels and can build on the subtask instruction following of π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a) and on the subtask descriptions and execution feedback that the authors of InternW0-Δ\Delta list as future extensions of its interface (Miao et al., 2026). First, the policy should follow the agent’s subgoals rather than only the task instruction. Second, it should be trained on the mid-episode states in which the agent transfers control, including disturbed and displaced ones. Third, it should end each segment on subgoal completion or failure, returning structured feedback to the agent and leaving any held object in a stable grasp. The agent, in turn, can be trained to delegate a subtask according to the policy’s competence on it and to use the proprioceptive state returned at every control transfer to keep a held object grasped.

Grounding exploratory experience into reusable memory and tools.

Within an episode, the agent diagnoses slips and displaced objects and revises its strategy, yet every new episode starts again from the same static prompt. Recent work turns such experience into reusable assets. Language-model programs compose perception and control APIs into robot behavior (Liang et al., 2023), and recent harnesses synthesize task programs around post-trained policies (Wang et al., 2026a), expose embodiment-specific primitives (Chen et al., 2026), or extend their control interfaces during deployment (Li et al., 2026c). To admit only experience that generalizes, recent work also validates candidate skills on held-out episodes (Lu et al., 2026) and isolates the evaluation from the agent that revises its own prompt and tools (Elmaaroufi et al., 2026). For embodied agents, two questions follow: which recoveries generalize beyond a single trial, and whether experience accumulated with one MLLM serves other MLLMs as well. The stated reasons of the agent offer a natural starting point, as each names a diagnosed failure together with the revised action that follows it. Validated pairs of failure and revision can be retained across episodes as memory or compiled into tools that wrap closed-loop control.

Transferring the agent’s exploratory and corrective strategies to smaller policies.

The recorded rollouts contain corrective strategies such as withdrawing for a wider view after a slip and lowering a sweep that missed the beans. The agent produces these strategies at the latency and token cost of a frontier MLLM. Distilling them into smaller models that run at deployment speed would pair failure states with the agent’s revised strategies and their outcomes, including corrections that did not succeed. Such distillation would thereby extend behavior cloning from trajectories toward the intentions behind them. Policies already improve from their own experience and from corrective interventions (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), and an LLM agent can run the cycle of training and evaluating a VLA without a human in the loop (Yu, 2026). Because agent rollouts carry the reason for every correction, they extend such training data to corrections that the agent discovers on its own.

Coupling geometric perception with active safety constraints in execution.

Precise contact and safe execution both depend on geometry that the agent infers from RGB views without depth. On insertion, threading, and seating, the agent has to judge the height of a surface, the clearance of a part, and the onset of contact from images, and its commands reach the robot without checks against the table, the workspace bounds, or the speed of the motion. The harness can therefore pair perception tools with a safety layer. Perception tools such as depth estimation, open-vocabulary detection and segmentation, and visual checks of the terminal state can estimate these quantities from the same camera views. The safety layer can check each command against workspace, reachability, and velocity limits and interrupt chunk execution on slip or collision. On real hardware, a queryable model of the robot’s body already lets an agent convert functional targets into control targets (Lou et al., 2026), and such a model can supply the kinematic limits that this safety layer enforces. Reporting safety events beside SR and score would let benchmarks measure this progress.

Limitations.

This report mainly studies the capability profile of one frontier MLLM, GPT-6-Astra, as the core of an agent on one simulated benchmark with synchronous execution, both under direct control and in a harness with two post-trained policies. Natural extensions include measuring the agent’s execution time, asynchronous execution in which the scene keeps evolving while the model deliberates, self-improvement of the agent with or without training the post-trained policy, a full evaluation of other frontier MLLMs as agent cores under the same protocol, and deployment on a physical robot. Appendix B.2 lists the protocol of each run.
