Appendix A Agent Interface and Prompts

This appendix reproduces the inputs and outputs of the agent from the stored records of the three configurations, and the system instructions and tool declarations from the code that each run executed. Omissions are marked […], other bracketed text replaces images, identifiers, and file paths or labels an excerpt, non-ASCII characters are transliterated, and line breaks within a paragraph result from typesetting.

A.1 Agent instructions and task prompt

System instructions.

Every agent session of the direct-control evaluation begins with the following system instructions, followed by instructions of the model host on returning images from tool calls. In both harness configurations, the list of prohibited actions ends with “or delegate to other agents”, and the query_icl paragraph that closes the task prompt below is inserted between the two parts.

You control one simulated EBench robot episode. Use only the supplied RGB and measured robot state and the declared robot tools. Do not read external files, use shell, browse, or delegate. The server judges success independently. Stop when it reports a terminal result or a budget is exhausted. Repeated observe at the same timestep shows the same scene. A closed gripper or finger contact alone does not prove a secure grasp. Choose continuous poses, motion timing and observation cadence yourself. [... instructions of the model host on returning images from tool calls ...]

Task prompt.

The first user turn consists of the task prompt, the demonstration (Appendix A.3), and the current observation. The excerpt below is the first turn of an episode of the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} on the bowl-to-plate test task. Under direct control, the agent received the same turn without the paragraph on execute_pi05 and the paragraph on query_icl.

Complete this single task yourself using the tools: Take out one of the three bowls and stack it on the plate. Robot: manip/lift2/R5a, two arms and a movable planar base. Left arm is left in the overlook view. EEF poses are local to each arm’s planner base: +X forward, +Y robot-left, +Z up; quaternion order wxyz. [...] There is no supplied depth, object pose or camera calibration. Only RGB and measured robot EEF/gripper/base state are available. [...] Use execute_eef sequentially, not parallel calls. Use observations to judge motion and object manipulation. The server determines task success independently. Do not start another episode. Resource limits: unlimited tool calls, physics deadline enforced by the server; no hard token limit; [...] When finished, state the observed outcome concisely. You may call execute_pi05 to delegate a manipulation segment to a learned policy. Choose when to delegate using the current scene. It replans every 30 steps and automatically returns control after the requested segment (at most 300 steps). The pi0.5 prompt is fixed for this task; always pass instruction=null and never invent a per-call prompt. Inspect its returned RGB/state and take over with EEF waypoints or delegate again. [...] The learned policy uses the same current three RGB cameras plus joint/gripper/base state; it receives no object ground truth or demonstration images. Manipulation guidance: after visually aligning, close at a stationary pose and allow settling. A nonzero finger gap on the table is contact evidence, not proof of a secure grasp. Test each grasp by lifting only 0.01 m first, using motion_steps=16 or more, then hold 8..16 steps and request the active wrist plus overlook views. [...] RGB inputs are downsampled: overlook 640x360, wrist 384x288; no crop or object annotation. The saved ICL demonstration remains available through query_icl throughout this episode. [...] Ground actions in the current RGB/state. [... the demonstration: annotation text and ten captioned keyframe images ...] END OF HISTORICAL DEMONSTRATION. The following images and measured state are the CURRENT episode. [...] Measured robot state (EEF poses in each arm’s planner base): {"state.gripper": [0.044, 0.044, 0.044, 0.044], "state.base": [0.0, 0.0, -0.0], "state.ee_pose": [[[0.1002, 0.0, 0.16349], [1.0, 0.0, 2e-05, -0.0]], [[0.1002, 0.0, 0.16349], [1.0, -0.0, 2e-05, -0.0]]], "timestep": 0} CURRENT RGB: overlook, 640x360 [image: overview camera] [... the left and right wrist views in the same format ...]

The harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta received the same turn with the following paragraph in place of the one on execute_pi05.

You may call execute_wam to delegate a manipulation segment to a learned policy. Choose when to delegate using the current scene. It replans every 10 steps and automatically returns control after the requested segment (at most 300 steps). The WAM prompt is fixed to this task’s instruction; always pass instruction=null and never invent a per-call prompt. [...] The learned policy uses the same current three RGB cameras plus robot state, and its own frames from earlier in this episode; it receives no object ground truth or demonstration images.

A.2 Tool interface

Table A.1 lists the agent’s tools with their argument schemas and their descriptions as declared to the model. Under direct control, the agent has the first three tools. The harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} adds execute_pi05 and query_icl, the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta adds execute_wam and query_icl, and the task prompt of each harness configuration adds the paragraphs on its two tools shown above. The declarations of the EEF tools and of query_icl are identical in every configuration that has them, and no other tool is declared.

A.3 Demonstration format

The demonstration enters the first turn as one text block followed by alternating keyframe captions and images, and the three configurations received the same demonstration. Table A.2 lists the parts of this text block for the bowl-to-plate task: the annotation of the source episode, a fixed paragraph on the interpretation of the records, and one numeric record per keyframe. Each record holds the measured EEF poses of the left arm ee0 and the right arm ee1 as position and wxyz quaternion, the summed finger gaps, and the base triplet, together with the exported action target.

A.4 Tool responses

Direct control.

Every tool response consists of a JSON receipt, a text line with the measured robot state, and a caption and an image for each requested camera. The receipts under direct control have the same structure, and no receipt in the three configurations compares a command with the measured state. The exchange below is call 20 of the episode whose first turn is shown above. The right arm holds a bowl, and the commanded position lies 0.107 m above the position reached. The receipt reports no error, so the shortfall is visible only from the measured state. The reason stated with the next call is appended.

[Request, call 20: execute_eef] {"cameras": ["overlook", "right_wrist"], "reason": "Lift the securely moving bowl slowly above sink.", "waypoints": [{"left": null, "right": {"xyz_m": [0.48996, -0.12997, 0.3], "quaternion_wxyz": [0.70722, 8e-05, 0.707, 0.00013], "gripper_m": [0, 0]}, "base_xy_yaw_deg": null, "motion_steps": 56, "steps": 64}]} [Response] {"executed_waypoints": [{"waypoint": 12, "executed_steps": 64, "measured_after": {"state.gripper": [0.044, 0.044, 0.00963, 0.0097], "state.base": [0.0003, 0.09162, -0.0], "state.ee_pose": [[[0.10034, -0.00058, 0.16485], [0.99998, 0.00116, 0.0035, -0.00427]], [[0.48621, -0.12846, 0.19264], [0.71538, -0.00048, 0.69874, 0.00032]]], "timestep": 1154}}], "remaining_tool_calls": null, "remaining_physics_steps": null, "reported_token_usage": {[...]}} Measured robot state (EEF poses in each arm’s planner base): [... the state of measured_after ...] CURRENT RGB: overlook, 640x360 [image: overview camera] CURRENT RGB: right_wrist, 384x288 [image: right wrist camera] [Reason stated with the next call, call 21: execute_eef] "Retract arm while raising to clear sink and reach a feasible carrying pose."

Post-trained policies.

A call to execute_pi05 returns the same structure, with a controller record in place of the waypoint receipts. The excerpt is call 1 of the same episode.

[Request, call 1: execute_pi05] {"cameras": ["overlook", "right_wrist"], "instruction": null, "reason": "Approach and align right hand with a bowl rim in the sink.", "steps": 120} [Response] {"executed_waypoints": [{"controller": "pi05", "requested_steps": 120, "executed_steps": 120, "inference_calls": 4, "control_returned_to": "agent", "episode_ended": false}], "remaining_tool_calls": null, "remaining_physics_steps": null, "reported_token_usage": {[...]}} Measured robot state (EEF poses in each arm’s planner base): {"state.gripper": [0.044, 0.044, 0.04398, 0.04398], "state.base": [-7e-05, 0.09306, -0.0], "state.ee_pose": [[[0.10035, 8e-05, 0.16352], [1.0, -0.00018, 0.00103, 0.00099]], [[0.35261, -0.03683, -0.00515], [0.70409, -0.00107, 0.71011, -0.00244]]], "timestep": 120} [... captions and images of the overview and right wrist cameras ...]

Appendix B Additional Benchmark Results

B.1 Tasks, leaderboard, and per-task comparisons

Tasks.

Figure B.1 shows the initial overview frame of one test episode of each of the 26 tasks, grouped by mobility and horizon, with the precision label of each task.

Leaderboard.

Table B.1 lists all entries of the EBench leaderboard by mobility group, including the entries not shown in Table 1: PICA-WAM (Zou et al., 2026), which fine-tunes OpenWAM-α\alpha with an action-alignment objective under visual perturbations, Vela, AMapbot, Cosmos3-Edge, and X-VLA, as well as InternW0-Δ\Delta with the evaluation of Appendix C. Among these 14 entries, the GPT-6-Astra-based agent under direct control ranks sixth in SR and fifth in score.

Per-task comparison.

Tables B.2 and B.3 give the SR and score of the agent and the eight post-trained policies on every test task. Relative to the best post-trained policy on each task in Table B.2, the agent’s SR is higher on three tasks, equal on five, and lower on eighteen. The three higher tasks are all mobile: Bookmark on book, Remote to holder, and Teacup, saucer & teapot. The five equal tasks are Dish, Pen, Perfume to cosmetics rack, Salt to spice rack, and Bottle, which no policy solves. The largest deficits occur on Dishwasher, Flip cup & collect cookies, and Glass into glassbox, where the agent reaches 5%, 10%, and 20% against 90% for the best post-trained policy. These three tasks involve an articulated object, coordinated use of both arms, and two-arm transfer with folding, respectively. The outcome breakdown separates two kinds of shortfall. On Tighten nut, Peg in hole, and Shop, no episode ends with a score of zero, so unsuccessful episodes receive partial credit for completed stages. On Gear installation and Utensils to holder, 15 and 13 of the 20 episodes end with a score of zero, so in these episodes the agent fails before completing the first scored stage.

Generalization dimensions.

Table B.4 gives SR and score in the four generalization dimensions. The Object dimension covers 24 tasks (120 episodes) and the other dimensions cover all 26 tasks (130 episodes), with five episodes per task and dimension.

Capability profile.

Figure B.2 compares the three highest-ranked systems among the agent and the eight post-trained policies by task group, as discussed in Section 5.2.

B.2 Evaluation protocol and event definitions

Evaluation records.

The horizon labels follow the corrected annotation of the benchmark designers, which differs from the grouping displayed on the leaderboard. When the agent ends an episode, the robot is held in place until the evaluation server determines the outcome, and 6 of the 49 direct-control episodes that the agent ended early succeeded during this hold. In the 56 direct-control episodes interrupted by an infrastructure failure, execution resumed from the unchanged simulator state in a new model thread initialized with the recorded action history and the current observations. The direct-control run evaluated Bottle and Shop with a step limit of 3,000 steps, whereas the benchmark’s current protocol, used by both harness configurations, sets a step limit of 5,000 steps for these two tasks. Within 3,000 steps, no episode of either task succeeds in any configuration. Under a step limit of 5,000 steps, the harness with policy solves 3 of 20 Shop episodes with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, 1 with InternW0-Δ\Delta, and none of Bottle. These episodes raise the overall SR of the harness configurations from 52.4% to 53.0% and from 55.8% to 56.0%, respectively.

Comparison protocol.

The results of the post-trained policies come from the public leaderboard, and those of InternW0-Δ\Delta alone come from the evaluation of Appendix C, which is its leaderboard entry. Comparisons between configurations of the agent, and between InternW0-Δ\Delta alone and its harness configuration, pair test episodes that were run at different times, and each configuration was run once per episode. The two harness configurations differ in the policy’s replanning interval and history as well as in the policy itself. The demonstrations include top-camera keyframes that the agent does not observe during execution, and for 31 of the 510 test episodes the demonstration is a recording of the test scene itself. The demonstration of Frame placement records the scene of four of its 20 test episodes. In the comparison with and without the demonstration (Appendix D.3), the two conditions were rendered with partly different textures. The recordings shown in the figures were selected to illustrate each behavior.

Grasp events.

The frequencies of disruptions and grip losses in Section 5 are computed from the finger gaps and commanded finger targets of both arms, recorded after every executed chunk of at most 8 physics steps, and from the stated reasons of all calls in the 510 direct-control episodes, including the segments resumed after an interruption. The finger gap of a hand is the summed opening of its two fingers, which reaches 88 mm when the hand is fully open, or 0.044 m per finger joint in state.gripper. A grip counts as closed on an object when, after a close command, the fingers come to rest between 2 and 80 mm apart over two samples at different timesteps, so that fingertips closed for pushing do not count, and as lost when the gap then collapses while the gripper is still commanded closed. A stated reason counts as reporting a disruption when it names a slip, a drop, a fall, a displacement, or a loss outside a preventive phrase such as “avoid” or “in case”, and words of an intended release such as “released” do not count. A loss counts as occurring in a grasp test when the reason of its call contains test, verify, confirm, or check as a whole word, or names a one-centimeter lift. In a random sample of 20 of the other losses, read together with the arm that loses the grip, 16 occur while an object is lifted or carried, 3 during door manipulation, and 1 during a placement.

Wrist and joint speed.

The speed measures of Section 5.5 use the same chunk records, from all 510 episodes under direct control and from the segments of π0.5\pi_{0.5} in all 510 episodes of the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, as listed in Table B.5. Between consecutive chunks of one command, the wrist rotation is the angle between the measured EEF orientations of an arm, and the joint speed is the largest change of any arm joint, both divided by the executed physics steps. The two controllers differ in the tail of the rotation rates, as a single command of the agent can complete a large reorientation within a few chunks. In 38 commands, spread over 31 episodes, a wrist turns through 90∘ or more within 24 physics steps, whereas no segment of π0.5\pi_{0.5} reaches this threshold. Most of these commands reorient or reposition the hand for a new approach. Fast joint motion shows the same contrast, as transitions above 0.08 rad per physics step occur more than five times as often under direct control.

B.3 Statistics

Aggregate differences between configurations are tested with a bootstrap over episodes within each task (5,000 resamples), which keeps the task composition fixed, while single-task differences use exact McNemar tests with Holm correction over the 26 tasks. For the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} against direct control, the 95% SR interval is [+2.0,+10.5][+2.0,+10.5] points when episodes are resampled within each task and [−2.5,+15.6][-2.5,+15.6] when tasks are resampled, and the score interval is [+0.006,+0.071][+0.006,+0.071]. By group, the SR intervals are [+6.8,+19.0][+6.8,+19.0] for long-horizon, [+3.6,+19.3][+3.6,+19.3] for tabletop, [−8.6,+3.2][-8.6,+3.2] for short-horizon, and [−11.3,+3.8][-11.3,+3.8] for high-precision tasks, and the score interval for high-precision tasks is [−0.163,−0.029][-0.163,-0.029]. The gain of the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta over direct control is significant under both resampling schemes, and on the short-horizon tasks this configuration also exceeds InternW0-Δ\Delta alone under both. After Holm correction over the 26 tasks, Glass into glassbox and Dishwasher rise significantly over direct control with either tool, Teacup, saucer & teapot falls significantly with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and against InternW0-Δ\Delta alone, the corresponding harness configuration gains significantly on Apple from shelf and Perfume to cosmetics rack while losing significantly on Shop.

Appendix C Harness Details

C.1 Post-trained policies

π0.5\pi_{0.5}.

The VLA tool is the π0.5\pi_{0.5} checkpoint fine-tuned on the EBench training set that appears as π0.5\pi_{0.5} on the leaderboard. A call executes 1–300 physics steps. The policy predicts 50 absolute joint and gripper targets per inference and replans every 30 steps under the fixed task instruction, and control returns to the agent after the requested steps with the same observations as an EEF command. The agent’s other tools and its prompt are those of Appendix A.

InternW0-Δ\Delta.

The WAM tool is an InternW0-Δ\Delta checkpoint (Miao et al., 2026) post-trained on EBench data for 77,150 steps. It represents the robot by joint and EEF state and, in 10 denoising steps, predicts 32 absolute joint and gripper targets and base motions, without generating video at inference, of which the first 10 are executed before the next inference. Each inference is conditioned on the three camera views, the proprioceptive state, the first frame of the episode, and the frame 32 steps earlier, under the fixed task instruction. The harness opens one model session per episode with the episode’s initial observation and executes each 10-action chunk as 8 and 2 steps, so that the frame 32 steps back is observed within a call. During the first inferences after the agent’s own control, that frame is unavailable and is padded as at an episode start, which affects 4,276 of the 69,054 inferences. The agent invokes the policy 8.1 times per episode, with 135 inferences, against 45 inferences of π0.5\pi_{0.5} in the configuration with π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Its standalone evaluation ran the same checkpoint with the same horizon, execution length, and history on all 510 test episodes with the original inference loop in which the earlier frame is always observed. This standalone evaluation is the entry of InternW0-Δ\Delta on the public leaderboard.

C.2 Additional results

Per-task results.

Table C.1 lists every task, ordered by the change in SR with π0.5\pi_{0.5}. The harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} exceeds both the agent under direct control and π0.5\pi_{0.5} alone on ten tasks and falls below the better of the two on thirteen. The ten tasks are Apple from shelf, Apple to fruit bowl, Bowl to plate, Dish, Flip cup & collect cookies, Make sandwich, Perfume to cosmetics rack, Glass into glassbox, Utensils to holder, and Shop. On Shop, it solves 3 of 20 episodes at the 5,000-step limit, against none for π0.5\pi_{0.5} alone and none for the direct-control run at 3,000 steps. The harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} loses 59 episodes that the agent solved under direct control. Of these, 11 come from Teacup, saucer & teapot, 6 from Fruit, and 5 each from Dish, Frame placement, and Microwave. Of the 91 episodes that it gains, 14 come from Glass into glassbox, 11 from Dishwasher, and 7 each from Detergent, Dish, and Flip cup & collect cookies. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, the harness exceeds both the agent under direct control and InternW0-Δ\Delta alone on eight tasks and falls below the better of the two on eleven. These eight tasks are Apple from shelf, Apple to fruit bowl, Bowl to plate, Dish, Flip cup & collect cookies, Make sandwich, Perfume to cosmetics rack, and Glass into glassbox. Of its 49 lost episodes, 8 come from Frame placement and 7 from Teacup, saucer & teapot. Of its 96 gained episodes, 14 come from Dishwasher, 13 from Glass into glassbox, and 11 from Flip cup & collect cookies.

Policy invocation measures.

The policy step share of an episode is the fraction of its executed physics steps that the policy executes, with EEF waypoints and gripper commands counted as the agent’s steps, and the share of a task is the mean over its episodes. For Figure 8a, the executed steps of each episode are divided into tenths, and the policy’s share is computed within each tenth. A policy invocation counts as a recovery request in Table 3 when its stated reason contains a whole-word match for a term of recovery, retrying, slipping, dropping, missing, displacement, re-approach, regrasp, or failure, as in “Recover slipped soap and realign a deeper centered grasp”. In a random sample of 40 calls coded in this way, 33 clearly ask the policy to recover from a disruption, 6 are ambiguous, and 1 is not a recovery request. Both harness configurations enter these measures with their Bottle and Shop episodes at 5,000 physics steps, as in Table 2.

Generalization dimensions.

Of the direct-control successes, the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} loses 43 of 126 on the Background and Mix dimensions against 16 of 111 on Object and Instruction (Fisher’s exact test, p=0.0005p=0.0005). With InternW0-Δ\Delta, the corresponding counts are 31 of 126 and 18 of 111 (p=0.15p=0.15).

Atomic skills.

Figure C.1 groups the per-task SRs of Table C.1 by the atomic skills that EBench annotates for each task. With π0.5\pi_{0.5} and InternW0-Δ\Delta alike, mean SR rises most on pushing, pressing, and pulling, by 21 to 70 percentage points, and sweeping improves by 17 and 24 points, respectively. Several tasks require more than one of these skills, as Dishwasher counts toward pushing, pulling, and sweeping, and Glass into glassbox accounts for most of the increase on pressing. Insertion is the only skill whose mean SR drops in both harness configurations, from 36.7% under direct control to 30.0% with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 26.7% with InternW0-Δ\Delta, while the two policies alone reach 23.3% and 18.3%. On handover, the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta reaches 45.0% against 65.0% for InternW0-Δ\Delta alone, its largest shortfall against the standalone policy among the skills.

Diagnosis.

An episode is classified as agent-terminated when the agent stops before the step limit without succeeding. Phrase rules assign its final message to either an unconfirmed completion claim or a reported failure, and a manual check of ten episodes per run confirms this assignment. Table C.2 follows every episode of the agent under direct control to the same scene in each harness configuration. The two harness configurations newly fail 108 episodes that the agent solved under direct control: 59 with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 49 with InternW0-Δ\Delta, on 85 distinct test episodes. Each of these episodes was read call by call, with the executor, the finger widths before and after, the base motion, and the agent’s stated reason of every call. Each was then assigned the incident after which the unfinished stage was never completed, as Table C.3 lists. Each agent-terminated episode is assigned the decisive incident preceding termination: a slip of the agent’s grasp, a loss around a policy segment, or an unmet stage behind a completion claim. A grip counts as held when the fingers come to rest between 2 and 80 mm apart over two samples at different timesteps while commanded closed, and as lost when it collapses while still commanded closed, and a reported slip is a stated reason coded as in Appendix B.2. An unmaintained grasp is an agent command that follows a policy segment and leaves an arm holding an object unspecified rather than closing it, so that the arm holds its measured finger width. Unmaintained grasps are counted per arm, so the 338 and 316 of Section 6.4 fall in 337 and 313 agent commands. The comparison in Section 6.4 counts unspecified holding arms after the agent’s own commands within the same configuration, and its stratified odds ratios use the Mantel–Haenszel estimator over the tasks on which both kinds occur.

Invocation and outcome.

Table C.5 compares successful and unsuccessful episodes of the two harness configurations. A motion command is a call of the EEF interface, the gripper command, or the policy, and a transition is a change of executor between two consecutive motion commands. Pooled over episodes, the number of transitions correlates with failure, with point-biserial correlations of r=0.42r=0.42 and r=0.44r=0.44, and within the 23 and 18 tasks with both outcomes, unsuccessful episodes make more transitions on 22 and 17 tasks (Wilcoxon signed-rank p=2.1×10−4p=2.1\times 10^{-4} and 1.5×10−51.5\times 10^{-5}). They also issue more motion commands on every one of these tasks, with fewer transitions per motion command on 17 of the 23 tasks (p=0.015p=0.015) and 15 of the 18 (p=0.06p=0.06). Episodes with a recovery request to the policy fail in 75.5% and 72.0% of cases, against 15.8% and 16.8% without one. Of the 251 and 239 episodes with a disruption report, 227 and 200 contain a recovery request.

Grip losses by executor.

Using the held state and the losses defined in Appendix B.2, every physics step between two samples of a held arm counts as a held arm-step of the executor of its call, and rates are given per 1,000 held arm-steps. The harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} holds objects for 278,496 arm-steps under the policy and 146,922 under the agent, with 176 and 321 losses, corresponding to rates of 0.63 and 2.18 per 1,000 held arm-steps. With InternW0-Δ\Delta, the corresponding values are 262,037 and 142,024 arm-steps, with 189 and 315 losses, or 0.72 and 2.22 per 1,000. Of the agent’s losses, 193 and 173 fall in grasp-test calls, and outside these calls the agent’s rates are 0.87 and 1.00. Under direct control, 811 losses over 447,352 held arm-steps give 1.81 per 1,000, and 1.05 outside grasp tests. Among the tasks with more than 2,000 held arm-steps under both executors, the agent’s rate exceeds the policy’s on 13 of 16 tasks with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 15 of 18 with InternW0-Δ\Delta.

C.3 API-equivalent cost

Prompt caching dominates the API-equivalent cost of every configuration (Table C.6). On each request, the agent resends the growing episode context, including the instructions, the demonstration, earlier observations, and tool results, so most of the input repeats an earlier prefix from the same episode and is billed at the cached-input rate. At the Standard tariff of GPT-6-Astra (USD 10, 1, 12.5, and 50 per million uncached input, cached input, cache-write, and output tokens), cached input covers 91.5–97.0% of the input tokens and still accounts for 44.0–70.5% of the cost per episode despite its tenfold discount. The recorded tokens cost USD 7.82 per episode under direct control and 2.63 and 3.06 in the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and with InternW0-Δ\Delta, corresponding to 16.82, 4.99, and 5.49 per success. For 44 direct-control episodes the final token record is missing, and the direct-control values here, in Figure 9, and in Section 5.3 count the recorded tokens. In all three configurations, token use rises with the number of tool calls, with Pearson correlations of 0.88 under direct control and 0.94 and 0.87 in the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} and with InternW0-Δ\Delta. No request exceeds the 272k input tokens above which the tariff raises input and cache rates twofold and output rates by half. Only the direct-control run records cache writes, because part of its episodes ran through the API rather than the subscription route, which reports none.

Appendix D Additional Qualitative Results

This appendix collects keyframes and prompt excerpts from the recordings of the direct-control evaluation. Appendix D.1 gives prompt-grounded cases, Appendix D.2 compares rollouts of the agent with those of two post-trained policies, and Appendix D.3 shows the episodes with and without the demonstration. Figure D.1 shows two successful episodes on tasks where the agent leads, as discussed in Section 5.2. Figure D.2 shows two unsuccessful episodes that end with partial credit, as discussed in Section 5.3. Figure D.3 shows three unsuccessful episodes of the kind analyzed in Section 5.3: two that stop at the final stage of a high-precision task and one that fails in a two-arm handover.

Figure D.4 shows three episodes with the safety-relevant behavior discussed in Section 5.5, and Figure D.5 shows the two ways in which the agent ends an unsuccessful episode itself, as discussed in Section 5.3.

D.1 Prompt-grounded cases

The stored prompts and stated reasons of unsuccessful episodes show how supplied guidance and its execution diverge. The first box below belongs to panel b of Figure 4, and the second shows a Fruit episode in which the agent follows the live instruction over the demonstration. Both list the guidance and the agent’s response.

D.2 Rollouts of the agent and post-trained policies

Recovery from subgoal disruptions.

Figure D.6 compares rollouts of the GPT-6-Astra-based agent, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and OpenWAM-α\alpha on the two tasks summarized in Section 5.6. In Teacup, saucer & teapot (Figure D.6a), the agent first approaches the cup handle and refines its wrist and gripper configuration over successive attempts before grasping and placing the cup onto the saucer. When subsequent manipulation of the teapot inadvertently displaces the cup from the saucer, the agent detects that the completed subgoal has been invalidated, re-grasps the cup, and restores it to the saucer rather than continuing the remaining action sequence. By contrast, π0.5\pi_{0.5} repeatedly approaches and retracts without completing the cup transfer, whereas OpenWAM-α\alpha fails to grasp the cup and proceeds to place the teapot onto the tray while leaving the cup off the saucer.

Precise contact in object manipulation.

In Glass into glassbox (Figure D.6b), although the agent uses both arms to place the glasses into the open case, its subsequent adjustments fail to fold the temples fully inward, leaving a protruding temple that prevents the lid from closing despite repeated corrective pushes. By comparison, π0.5\pi_{0.5} places the glasses into the case and folds both temples compactly (though leaving the lid open), while OpenWAM-α\alpha completes both temple folding and lid closure.

D.3 In-context learning

Figure D.7 shows keyframes from the paired evaluation with and without the annotated demonstration across all 20 test episodes of Frame placement and Gear installation (Section 5.6). On Frame placement (1/20 successes zero-shot vs. 13/20 with the demonstration, mean score 0.283 vs. 0.800), under zero-shot control the agent reaches and displaces the frame, but repeatedly adjusts its approach trajectory and wrist orientation without achieving stable placement. When conditioned on the demonstration, the agent coordinates both grippers to hold and transfer the frame in 17 of 20 episodes (including all 13 successful episodes, compared with 1 of 20 under zero-shot control) and positions the frame upright against the pen holder (Figure D.7a). On Gear installation (3/20 successes under both conditions), without the demonstration the agent grasps and lifts the gear but leaves it outside the assembly region, whereas with the demonstration it brings the gear between the two mounted gears and lowers it, but it scores no stage in 15 of the 20 episodes (Figure D.7b).

Appendix E Case Studies in the Harness with Policy

The direct-control episodes of Appendix D illustrate three failure categories: an unconfirmed completion claim, an object lost beyond the reachable workspace, and a long-horizon task that ends with partial credit. Figure E.1 presents three episodes in the harness with policy on scenes that the agent solved under direct control, covering an unconfirmed completion claim, an unrecovered object loss, and a completed stage undone by a subsequent policy segment. The call-by-call records report the executor, the physics steps, the finger opening as defined in Appendix B.2, and the agent’s stated reason.

Figure E.2 compares, on one scene each of Glass into glassbox and Teacup, saucer & teapot, the agent under direct control with the harness with π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Sections 6.3 and 6.4).

E.1 Division of labor

The stated reasons below come from the successful Flip cup & collect cookies episode discussed in Section 6.5.

E.2 Verifying physical completion

Like the direct-control Dishwasher episode of Figure D.5a, the Gear installation episode of Figure E.1a with π0.5\pi_{0.5} ends with an unconfirmed completion claim. The agent closes the left hand on the gear hub and lifts the gear by 1 cm (calls 3 and 4, finger opening 29.9 and 30.0 mm), then invokes π0.5\pi_{0.5} for transport and seating in three segments of 180, 180, and 120 physics steps. In the second segment (call 6, stated reason “Continue fine alignment and seating of the blue gear on the middle axis”), π0.5\pi_{0.5} opens the left fingers from 29.9 to 86.2 mm beside the large gear. The agent then withdraws the open left hand and closes it (calls 8 and 9), requesting only the overview image for both commands, in which the board occupies a small part of the frame. It ends the episode at 828 physics steps with the final message “The blue gear is in the middle position between the white gears and remained there after the hand withdrew”, and the episode scores 0.5. On the same scene, the agent under direct control releases the gear, inspects the assembly from a more vertical wrist view (call 12), re-approaches the hub to correct a forward offset from the spindle (call 13), and withdraws only after the spindle becomes visible through the gear bore (call 16), solving the scene in 821 physics steps.

E.3 Unrecovered object losses

In the recorded episodes, an object that leaves the reachable workspace is not recovered for the rest of the episode, as when the apple of Figure D.4b falls and the agent under direct control searches outside the workspace. In the Detergent episode of Figure E.1b, the agent drops the first bottle to the floor when it resumes control during a bimanual handover. InternW0-Δ\Delta closes the right hand on the first bottle while the left hand still holds it (call 4, 250 physics steps), ending with a fully closed finger command and a measured finger opening of 32.9 mm. The agent then opens the left hand (call 5) without commanding the right hand to stay closed, so the right fingers remain at their measured opening of 32.9 mm (Section 6.4), and the bottle tilts in the right hand while the left hand opens. In the 1 cm lift test that follows (call 6, stated reason “Check whether the receiving hand retained the bottle using a small lift”), the right fingers close from 32.8 to 2.2 mm within the first 8 physics steps, and the bottle falls from the counter to the floor. InternW0-Δ\Delta places the two other bottles in the basket by physics step 2,348, but the next 20 calls (calls 19 to 38) and 2,020 physics steps fail to recover the bottle on the floor: seven EEF waypoints directed toward the floor end 11 to 20 cm from their targets, and three InternW0-Δ\Delta segments of 300 physics steps each end with the fingers closed at 0.0 to 0.1 mm. The agent ends the episode at 4,368 physics steps with the final message “The blue/red bottle fell to the floor, and recovery attempts failed”, and the episode scores 0.67. Under direct control, the agent solves the same scene in 1,681 physics steps, carrying each bottle in the left hand without a transfer between the hands.

E.4 Preserving completed stages

Figure D.2b shows a Bottle episode under direct control that ends with partial credit. In the harness with policy, a policy segment can also undo a stage that is already complete, because the post-trained policy receives the fixed task instruction without a record of the completed stages, as analyzed in Section 6.7. In the Teacup, saucer & teapot episode of Figure E.1c, five segments of π0.5\pi_{0.5} at the cup (calls 2, 4, and 5) and at the teapot (calls 22 and 24) end with the right hand empty and take 540 of the first 1,602 physics steps. Between those segments, the agent completes the cup placement itself, grasping the cup, releasing it on the saucer at physics step 994 (call 20), and verifying the placement (call 21). Its own handle grasp of the teapot holds at a 9.6 mm finger opening in the lift test (call 31), but the fingers close to 0.0 mm as the teapot is lifted clear (call 32). The agent invokes π0.5\pi_{0.5} for recovery with the stated reason “reapproach shifted handle with learned alignment” (call 34, 180 physics steps). In this segment, the hand descends beside the teapot, the saucer tips up under it, and the cup falls and comes to rest upside down on the table, undoing the earlier placement. The agent then tests the new contact as a teapot grasp (call 36) and releases it (call 37), and the episode runs until the step limit of 2,000 physics steps inside a final segment of π0.5\pi_{0.5} with the stated reason “Recover displaced cup and saucer” (call 38). The episode scores 0. Under direct control, the agent solves the same scene in 1,631 physics steps.

E.5 Recovery after delegated handovers

Figure E.3 shows a Shop episode in the harness with InternW0-Δ\Delta that fails although InternW0-Δ\Delta alone completes the same scene in 4,166 physics steps. The failure begins when the small carton drops in a handover between the hands that the agent delegates to the policy. The agent first lets the policy retry and then takes over, placing the carton on the destination belt with its own waypoints. After a can also slips in a later delegated handover, the agent again takes over, this time to secure the long box. Both recoveries succeed, but together with the failed handovers they use up the budget, so the episode reaches the 5,000-step limit while the agent carries a can across the scanner.
